findings.title: Backup code can bypass password verification when a dummy TOTP code is also supplied
findings.body: Password verification only runs when `!credentials.totpCode`, while the new branch at line 131 authorizes solely on `credentials.backupCode` and ignores the TOTP value. An attacker who obtains one backup code can call the credentials provider directly with that code plus any non-empty totpCode (e.g. "x") and an empty/wrong password: the password check is skipped and the backup-code check succeeds, so a second-factor recovery code becomes a complete password replacement. Password must be verified whenever a password account is logging in, regardless of which second factor is presented, or the second-step flow must use a trustworthy proof that password verification already occurred.

findings.title: Single-use backup code can be replayed by concurrent logins
findings.body: Consumption is a non-atomic read-modify-write: authorize() reads and decrypts user.backupCodes, checks indexOf, then updates the row at lines 149-156. Two concurrent sign-in requests using the same code can both read the pre-consumption array and both pass the index check before either update commits, violating the documented exactly-once property and allowing one leaked code to create multiple sessions. The consumption needs an atomic/conditional update, transaction with row locking, or equivalent compare-and-swap so only one request can claim a code.

findings.title: Users who enabled 2FA before this feature can never obtain backup codes
findings.body: Backup codes are only generated in setup, and setup returns TwoFactorAlreadyEnabled for anyone with twoFactorEnabled already true. All pre-existing 2FA users therefore have backupCodes = null forever unless they disable and re-enroll in 2FA; the new MissingBackupCodes error even tells them to generate codes in settings, where no generation/regeneration endpoint or UI exists. This leaves the recovery flow permanently unusable (and the error text misleading) for the population most likely to need it.

findings.title: Backup-code comparison rejects valid codes typed in different case or with surrounding whitespace
findings.body: Generated codes are lowercase hex (crypto.randomBytes(5).toString('hex') in setup) and are shown/downloaded in that form, but verification only strips '-' before a case-sensitive indexOf; the same logic is used in the disable endpoint. A user who manually transcribes a code in uppercase (as suggested by the XXXXX-XXXXX placeholder in BackupCode.tsx) or pastes it with leading/trailing whitespace gets IncorrectBackupCode and may be locked out, even though hex case is semantically irrelevant. Normalize input with trim().toLowerCase() (and server-side, not just in the form) before comparison in both verification paths.

findings.title: No test exercises actually logging in or disabling 2FA with a backup code, or its single-use property
findings.body: The added e2e coverage only clicks download/copy/close on the code display, and line 12 explicitly defers login and disable-with-backup-code tests. Nothing proves a generated code authenticates, that a wrong code is rejected at login, that a consumed code cannot be reused (including the second login attempt), or that a code works in DisableTwoFactorModal. This is the security-critical behavior of the PR, so at least login-with-code plus reuse-rejection should be covered before merging.
